paragraphs.name: 8d2d
paragraphs.text: Getting Singapore making with the micro:bit
Behind the scenes of the Digital Maker Programme

paragraphs.name: 509c
paragraphs.text: One of our first micro:bit-powered robots, which has since wandered into some corner of the office. We’ll find you one day, kiddo!

paragraphs.name: 10b5
paragraphs.text: Since the beginning of the year, we’ve been working with the Infocomm Media Development Authority of Singapore to launch the Digital Maker Programme. The programme aims to take thousands of BBC micro:bits, fling them at anyone with a pulse, and see what awesome things people come up with. (We might have paraphrased a little here.)

paragraphs.name: 58aa
paragraphs.text: In all seriousness, we do feel very strongly about the programme, and care deeply about what it’s actually trying to achieve, which is to introduce a new, meaningful kind of creative digital literacy in the public. It’s the feeling that learners get when they start coding and tinkering—of empowerment, of “hey, I can do this!”, of wanting to make something of their own—that spurs them to go on to learn more and spend hundreds of hours making ridiculous home-made arcade cabinets.

paragraphs.name: 5d82
paragraphs.text: We’ve spent the better part of this year up to our knees in micro:bits and electronic parts, and we’d like to take some time to share what we’re doing for this programme.

paragraphs.name: d02f
paragraphs.text: First, we’ve created our very own micro:bit kits for our classes and for sale to the public. We developed a custom Breakout Board, in collaboration with ScienceScope UK, to make connecting external components (affordable Octopus bricks) a breeze for beginners and experienced tinkerers, and we’re building custom kits for all age groups and experience levels. Links below go to our Tinkercademy micro:bit info page, and our Get Hacking micro:bit store.

Tinkercademy micro:bit info page
We developed our very own Breakout Board and kit for the micro:bit. Find out how to use the kit, and read about our projects here! tinkercademy.com

paragraphs.name: 1a42
paragraphs.text:
Get Hacking with the Tinkercademy microbit collection
Become Digital Makers with our microbit kits and components!gethacking.com

paragraphs.name: e3ef
paragraphs.text: Second, we’re bringing the micro:bit, intro coding, electronics prototyping, and digital making into classrooms, with classes for students through the Code for Fun programme, and for teachers through Microsoft Singapore.

Third, we’re bringing interactive micro:bit projects to community events such as Tech Saturday, Children’s Season at the National Museum, and Singapore Maker Faire 2017. You may have seen the programmable robots and air cannons—come by Science Centre on 22 & 23 July for Maker Faire to see a digital maker extravaganza.

paragraphs.name: f3c0
paragraphs.text: “How old are you? 3 years old? Maybe you can’t code this yet, but here, hold this soldering iron…”

paragraphs.name: 21a2
paragraphs.text: Fourth, we’ve written, and are refining, iOS and Android apps for our micro:bit tutorials. You can download them to try—please send us your feedback!

paragraphs.name: 6f7f
paragraphs.text:
Get Hacking on electronics with micro:bit on the App Store
Read reviews, compare customer ratings, see screenshots and learn more about Get Hacking on electronics with micro:bit…itunes.apple.com

paragraphs.name: df5e
paragraphs.text:
Get Hacking - Android Apps on Google Play
Get Hacking with the micro:bit!play.google.com

paragraphs.name: 01c6
paragraphs.text: Finally, our most ambitious project to date: we’re writing a new block-based programming language for makers. Here’s the premise: You shouldn’t have to know how to code to make simple input-output devices using micro-controllers like Arduino or micro:bit. Why can’t you just fit an input with an output, and have things work as expected? Soon, with our new language, you’ll be able to. (We hope. Fingers crossed!)
(Also, this is the project we alluded to in our first post, where the technology stack is “a healthy mix of C++, JavaScript, and staring at one another suspiciously”.)

In closing, here’s the quote we provided for IMDA’s press release. We normally write these up two minutes before the deadline, then hope nobody notices we sent unintelligible garblish, but this one actually sums up our goals for this programme:

paragraphs.name: 243e
paragraphs.text: We love tinkering with technology and like to share this joy with others. Through conducting coding and electronics classes over the past 6 years, we have met many kids and adults who were really excited about making with technology, but wish they didn’t have to first wrap their head around coding. The Digital Maker programme and the micro:bit present a unique opportunity for us to create a set of tools that addresses this by allowing coders and non-coders alike to get down to digital making right away.

paragraphs.name: c183
paragraphs.text: So that’s what we’ve been up to lately. Questions? Comments? Suggestions? Puzzled glances? Please get in touch at hello@tinkertanker.com! We check our email when we aren’t lost in a pile of parts, or trying to put out fires from the laser cutter.

paragraphs.name: 388e
paragraphs.text: The micro:bit with Breakout Board and a… fan you control using two glasses of water, maybe? We dunno ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
